svg.title: Cross-domain multicast: four approaches, from single domain to SSM between enterprises and carriers
svg.desc: Four stacked approaches with complexity rising. Single domain: everything solved inside one PIM domain, lowest complexity. MSDP across domains: ASM, domains exchange source-active messages and each builds its own tree, medium to high complexity, traditional carrier-provided multicast. MBGP plus MSDP: MBGP supplies the multicast RPF path while MSDP supplies source discovery, highest complexity, used when multicast needs a path separate from unicast. SSM across domains: no RP and no MSDP, only source-prefix reachability from ordinary BGP unicast, lowest complexity and the recommended option. A right column shows what has to be true for each option to work. A footer explains why inter-domain multicast is hard: RPF requires the source to be reachable by a multicast route, and there is no global source discovery mechanism, so every approach is a way of manufacturing that knowledge.
svg.text: Crossing a domain boundary: four answers, ordered by what they cost you
Every one of them is really a way of answering the same question - how does the far side learn that a source exists?
One PIM domain, one RP set, one address plan.
If a design "needs" this to be two domains,
the boundary was drawn in the wrong place.
Each domain keeps its own RP and its own tree;
SAs are exchanged so RP-B learns RP-A's sources.
MBGP (SAFI 2) makes multicast RPF follow a
different path than unicast; MSDP still finds sources.
Two policies that must stay in step, forever.
No RP and no MSDP: the receiver already names
the source, so only source-prefix reachability matters.
Why this is genuinely hard, and not just unfamiliar
RPF accepts a packet only if the source is reachable through the incoming interface. Between domains there is no shared RP and no global "who is sending" registry -
so ASM needs MSDP to invent one, MBGP to bend the path, and SSM to remove the need entirely. Notice the trend: the newest option is also the simplest one.
